3267.t: δια- (dĭă-) + Proto-Indo-European *kón-os, from *ken- (“to set oneself in motion”).

3296.t: Possibly from a nasalized variant of Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (“to shine”), but problematic due to said nasalization.

3234.t: Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *swel-, *sel- (“firewood, wood, beam”), and compared with Latin silva (“forest”), English sill, Latvian sile (“trough”).

3264.t: From δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, choose”).

3243.t: Related to μακεδνός (măkednós, “tall, slim”), which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ḱ- (“long, slender”).

3253.t: From the root of βαίνω (baínō, “to go”).

3277.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷʰḗr, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwer-. Cognates include Latin ferus (“wild, savage”), and Old Church Slavonic звѣрь (zvěrĭ, “wild animal”).

3276.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰermos Proto-Hellenic *kʷʰermós Ancient Greek θερμός From Proto-Hellenic *kʷʰermós, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer-mo-s (“warm”), from the root *gʷʰer-.

3268.t: Typically derived as a verbal noun (“holding”) of δράσσομαι (drắssomai, “to hold, to seize”).

3218.t: Stem ἱλα- as in ἱλάσκομαι (hīlắskomai, “to appease”), ἵλαος (hílaos, “gracious”) + -ρός (-rós).

3216.t: From ἰατρός (īātrós, “physician”), from ἰάομαι (iáomai, “I cure, treat”).

3251.t: From Proto-Hellenic *aulós, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlós, nominalization of *h₂ewlo- (“tube, hollow, channel”).

3232.t: Mediopassive of ὑποκρίνω (hŭpokrī́nō), from ὑπο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + κρίνω (krī́nō, “to separate, judge, decide”).

3291.t: From κλάω (klắō, “to break”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

3297.t: From Proto-Hellenic *lā́tʰā, from Proto-Indo-European *léh₂dʰeh₂, from *leh₂- (“to be concealed”) (whence λανθάνω (lanthánō)).

3256.t: Verbal formation from the same root as βλάβη (blắbē, “hurt, damage”), and traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥kʷyéti, from Proto-Indo-European *melkʷ- (“to damage”).

3292.t: Unknown; presumedly of foreign or substrate origin.

3271.t: From εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agentive suffix).

3260.t: By surface analysis, γνωρ(ίζω) (gnōr(ízō), “to make known; learn, discover”) + -ιμος (-imos). Also substantivised.

3257.t: Of imitative origin, but the exact Proto-Indo-European root is unclear.

3229.t: From relative ὅς (hós) (or from its stem) + indefinite ποτέ (poté). Compare ὅτε (hóte).

3235.t: Possible Greek relations, even if ruled out by Beekes as highly unlikely, are the verbal present form ἔθει (éthei), the participle ἔθων (éthōn, “damaging, plaguing; pushing, tossing (?)”) and the nouns ἔθρις (éthris, “castrated ram”), ἔθειρα (étheira,…

3222.t: Back-formation from ὄλισθον (ólisthon), itself inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sléydʰ-t ~ *h₃slidʰ-ént, from *h₃sleydʰ- (“to slip, slide”).

3258.t: From βαστάζω (bastázō, “I lift up, I raise”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

3298.t: Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“hair, wool”), like Latin vellus (“fleece”), or from the same root of Ancient Greek εὔληρα (eúlēra, “rein”), Latin lōrum (“thong”) and Old Armenian լար (lar, “rope”).

3211.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁élḱos (“wound, illness, ulcer”), from the root *h₁elḱ-. Cognate with Latin ulcus (“ulcer”) and Sanskrit अर्श॑स् (árśas, “hemorrhoids”)).

3231.t: Probably a compound of ὁμοῦ (homoû, “together”) + the ἀρ- (ăr-) found in ἀραρίσκω (ărărĭ́skō, “to fasten; to join”), i.e. "joined together" > "one who is forced to accompany" > "pledge, hostage".

3294.t: Probably from Pre-Greek, with intensive reduplication.

3254.t: From Proto-Indo-European *gʷeh₂- (“to step”), the same root of ἔβην (ébēn).

3224.t: This verb's formation is similar to ἀρτάω (artáō), οὐτάω (outáō) and φοιτάω (phoitáō). It is commonly assumed that the verbal adjective ὀπτός (optós, “baked, roasted”) forms its basis.

3261.t: Probably Proto-Hellenic *gémō, from Proto-Indo-European *gém-e-ti, a simple thematic present belonging to the root *gem- (“to take, seize”).

3240.t: Learned borrowing from Biblical Hebrew תָּבוֹר.
